checks: The transformed endpoint centers are a−c and −a−c with half-length ℓ, and the middle center is c with half-length R=ℓ+2c. The listed ordering of the endpoint centers has no effect on their sum.
The identity T_L(−t)=2L−T_L(t) gives the contribution 2L+D_L(b,r) for each transformed center b. Oddness gives the signed bracket in the proof.

The derivative is the sum of the two stated clipping indicators almost everywhere. Its bounds give a nonnegative middle term of at most 2c and an endpoint bracket of at most 4c, proving the upper bound.

For r≤ℓ+c, both middle arguments are in the clipping interval and their difference is 2c. For r>ℓ+c the open derivative intervals for the endpoint law have gap 2(r−ℓ)>2c, so an interval of length 2c cannot meet both. This proves the lower bound, including c=0 and all clipping endpoints.

That theorem determines the pointwise and maximum depth for unpadded three-interval fibers. Its minima over slopes do not give this paired two-sided estimate for every fixed slope.

The ordinary centered-law and symmetric-noise bound requires a convex uniform or centered concave law and gives a different estimate. Here the law is the sampled three-interval mass in the same slope, paired about the mark c.
